title: A Record-Breaking Parasite Outbreak Is Over, But Where Did It Come From?
summary:
What would you do if you had watery diarrhea with "frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements"? That's how the CDC describes the illness caused by a microscopic parasite called cyclospora. This year, the U.S. had a record-breaking outbreak: nearly 20,000 lab-confirmed cases since May 1. That's more than 16 times the number from the same time last year. More than 6,100 suspected cases were also reported. The worst previous year was 2019, with about 4,700 cases.

The outbreak was linked to iceberg lettuce from central Mexico, served at restaurants like Taco Bell. The company Taylor Farms recalled thousands of packaged salad products. But thousands of other cases were never linked to that lettuce. And here's the mystery: cyclospora spreads through human feces. How did sewage contaminate enough food to sicken so many people? "This contamination can happen if produce is grown in soil or comes into contact with water that has been contaminated," said Ellen Shumaker, a food safety expert at North Carolina State University.

Michigan was hit hardest, with the most cases and two deaths. The FDA has now ended its on-site inspections in Mexico, but samples are still being analyzed. The outbreak also showed a bigger problem: the U.S. is doing fewer international inspections to catch contaminated produce before it reaches your plate. So while this outbreak is over, the question of how to prevent the next one remains.
why_it_matters: The food on your plate often travels thousands of miles to reach you, so checking how it is grown and washed is a job that protects your family and your school cafeteria.

background_read: Cyclospora (a tiny one-celled parasite too small to see) causes watery diarrhea that can last for weeks, and people usually get it from fresh produce that was grown or washed with contaminated water.
Two U.S. agencies work on outbreaks like this: the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which tracks diseases) and the FDA (Food and Drug Administration, which checks food and medicines).
The United States has had smaller cyclospora outbreaks before, often tied to fresh produce and herbs grown in Mexico.
Article_Structure: WHO: The CDC and the FDA, the food company Taylor Farms, restaurants like Taco Bell, and the thousands of people who got sick.
WHAT: A record-breaking cyclospora outbreak with nearly 20,000 confirmed cases, linked to iceberg lettuce but with thousands of other cases never linked to it.
WHERE: Across the United States, with Michigan hit hardest, and the lettuce traced back to central Mexico.
WHY: It shows how germs on a farm far away can sicken people here, and that fewer international inspections make it harder to catch the next outbreak early.

perspectives.description: The CDC and FDA tracked the cases, ended on-site inspections in Mexico, and are still analyzing samples to figure out how the parasite got into the food.
Ellen Shumaker says produce can pick up the parasite from contaminated soil or water, so farms need to watch how food is grown and washed, not just the final product.
They point out that the U.S. is doing fewer international inspections, meaning contaminated produce may reach people's plates before anyone catches the problem.
